stem: What is meant by **variation**?

options.content: The differences between individuals of different species
options.rationale: Variation, in this sense, is between individuals of the same species.

options.content: A change in the base sequence of DNA
options.rationale: That is a gene mutation, one cause of variation.

options.content: The differences between individuals of the same species
options.rationale: For example, different heights or blood groups among people.

options.content: The way a species changes over millions of years
options.rationale: That is evolution, which depends on variation.

explanation: Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species, such as differences in height, mass or blood group between people.
hints: Think of the differences between students in your class.

stem: Which feature shows **discontinuous** variation?

options.content: ABO blood group
options.rationale: There are four distinct groups and no intermediates.

options.content: Height
options.rationale: Height varies over a range, with many intermediate values.

options.content: Body mass
options.rationale: Mass varies continuously between two extremes.

options.content: Length of a leaf
options.rationale: Leaf length can take any value within a range.

explanation: ABO blood group has only four phenotypes (A, B, AB and O) with nothing in between, so it shows discontinuous variation. Height, mass and leaf length show continuous variation.
hints: Which feature falls into a few separate groups?

stem: Which feature shows **continuous** variation?

options.content: Whether a person can roll their tongue
options.rationale: There are only two categories: can or cannot.

options.content: The length of maize cobs in a field
options.rationale: Cob lengths form a range between two extremes, with many intermediates.

options.content: The sex of calves born on a farm
options.rationale: Calves are male or female, with no intermediates.

options.content: Whether pea seeds are round or wrinkled
options.rationale: There are two distinct categories.

explanation: Cob length can take any value within a range, from short to long, so it shows continuous variation. Tongue rolling, sex and seed shape fall into distinct categories.
hints: Which feature could be measured with a ruler and take any value?

stem: True or false: in a histogram showing continuous variation, the bars touch each other.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. The class intervals run on from one another, so the bars touch.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Continuous data are grouped into classes that follow on from each other, so the bars of a histogram touch. Bar charts for discontinuous data have gaps.

explanation: In a histogram the classes are continuous (for example 10.0–11.9 cm, then 12.0–13.9 cm), so the bars touch. A bar chart for discontinuous data has separate bars because there are no values between the categories.
hints: Is there a gap between one class of lengths and the next?

stem: State the type of variation shown by the ABO blood groups.

rejected.feedback: Blood groups fall into four distinct categories with no intermediates, so the variation is discontinuous.
Blood groups fall into four distinct categories with no intermediates, so the variation is discontinuous.
Blood group is genetic, but the type of variation is discontinuous.

explanation: There are only four blood groups (A, B, AB and O) and no intermediates, so the ABO blood groups show discontinuous variation.
hints: Are there any 'in-between' blood groups?

stem: What usually causes **continuous** variation?

options.content: A single gene only
options.rationale: A single gene usually gives a few distinct phenotypes (discontinuous variation).

options.content: The environment only
options.rationale: Genes also matter: tall parents tend to have tall children.

options.content: Mutations in body cells only
options.rationale: Mutations create new alleles, but continuous variation comes from many genes acting with the environment.

options.content: Many genes together with the environment
options.rationale: Each gene adds a small effect, and the environment adds more.

explanation: Continuous variation is usually caused by many genes, each with a small effect, together with environmental factors such as food, light, water and mineral ions.
hints: Can diet affect your height? Can your genes?

stem: Decide whether each feature shows continuous or discontinuous variation.

left.content: Body mass of goats in a herd
Blood group of students in a class
Daily milk yield of cows in a dairy herd
Ability of people to roll their tongue
Sex of chicks hatched in an incubator

explanation: Mass and milk yield can take any value within a range (continuous). Blood group, tongue rolling and sex fall into a few distinct categories with no intermediates (discontinuous).
hints: Could the feature be measured on a scale, or only sorted into groups?

stem: Complete the sentences about variation.

payload.template: Continuous variation gives a {{blank:range}} of phenotypes between two extremes. Discontinuous variation gives a limited number of phenotypes with no {{blank:inter}}. Continuous data are shown on a {{blank:graph}}, with the bars touching.

explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes, shown on a histogram with touching bars. Discontinuous variation: a few distinct phenotypes with no intermediates, shown on a bar chart with gaps.
hints: Discontinuous means there are gaps between the categories.

stem: A farmer near Gwanda weighed eight young goats. Their masses, in kg, were: 32.5, 28.0, 35.5, 30.0, 41.0, 26.5, 38.0 and 33.5. Calculate the **mean** mass, to one decimal place.
explanation: Mean $= \dfrac{265.0}{8} = 33.125$, which is $33.1\ \text{kg}$ to one decimal place.
hints: Add all the masses, then divide by the number of goats.

stem: The heights of ten maize seedlings, in mm, were: 45, 62, 58, 71, 39, 66, 52, 49, 75 and 60. Calculate the **range** of the heights.
explanation: Range = largest − smallest $= 75 - 39 = 36\ \text{mm}$.
workedSolution:
1. Largest height = 75 mm; smallest = 39 mm.
2. Range $= 75 - 39 = 36\ \text{mm}$.
hints: The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values.

stem: In a class of 36 students, 27 could roll their tongues. What percentage of the class could **not** roll their tongues?
explanation: $36 - 27 = 9$ students could not roll their tongues: $\dfrac{9}{36} \times 100 = 25\%$.
hints: First find how many students could not roll their tongues.

stem: A student surveys the blood groups of 60 people. Which type of graph should she draw?

options.content: A histogram with touching bars
options.rationale: Histograms are for continuous data grouped into classes.

options.content: A bar chart with a gap between the bars
options.rationale: Blood groups are separate categories with nothing in between.

options.content: A line graph joining the points
options.rationale: A line would suggest values between the groups, which do not exist.

options.content: A scatter graph
options.rationale: Scatter graphs compare two measured variables.

explanation: Blood group is discontinuous: there are four distinct categories. Discontinuous data are shown on a bar chart with separate bars.
hints: Are blood groups measured on a scale, or counted in categories?

stem: Rudo and Rumbi are identical twins, so they have the same genes. At the age of 20, Rudo is 6 kg heavier than Rumbi. What is the best explanation?

options.content: They inherited different alleles for body mass.
options.rationale: Identical twins have exactly the same alleles.

options.content: Body mass shows discontinuous variation.
options.rationale: Mass shows continuous variation.

options.content: Their environment differed, for example in diet or exercise.
options.rationale: With the same genes, differences must come from the environment.

options.content: One of them must have a mutation in every body cell.
options.rationale: There is no evidence of mutation; diet and exercise affect mass.

explanation: Identical twins have the same genotype, so differences between them are caused by the environment, such as diet, exercise or illness. Body mass shows continuous variation, which is affected by both genes and environment.
hints: If the genes are identical, what else can differ?

stem:
Students measured the lengths of 40 maize cobs from one field near Chinhoyi. The table shows their results.

| Length of cob / cm | 10.0–12.9 | 13.0–15.9 | 16.0–18.9 | 19.0–21.9 | 22.0–24.9 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of cobs | 3 | 8 | 15 | 10 | 4 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which type of variation is shown by cob length?

options.content: Continuous, because the lengths form a range with intermediates
options.rationale: Lengths can take any value between the extremes.

options.content: Discontinuous, because the lengths are grouped into five classes
options.rationale: The classes are chosen by the students; the lengths themselves are continuous.

options.content: Discontinuous, because only 40 cobs were measured
options.rationale: The sample size does not decide the type of variation.

options.content: Continuous, because cob length is controlled by one gene
options.rationale: Continuous variation usually involves many genes and the environment.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of cobs that were **19.0 cm or longer**.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** environmental factors that could cause the variation in cob length within one field.

points.description: Any one: water supply / rainfall reaching each plant
A second factor: mineral ions or fertiliser in the soil; light (shading); competition from weeds or close spacing; damage by pests or disease

parts.explanation: Plants in different parts of the field may receive different amounts of water, and the soil may contain different amounts of mineral ions (for example where fertiliser was spread unevenly). Shading, competition from weeds and attack by pests such as stalk borers could also reduce the growth of some plants.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Which type of graph should the students draw to show these results?

options.content: A bar chart with gaps between the bars
options.rationale: Gaps suit categories; these classes run on from one another.

options.content: A histogram with the bars touching
options.rationale: The data are continuous and grouped into equal classes.

options.content: A pie chart
options.rationale: A pie chart shows proportions of categories, not the shape of a continuous distribution.

options.content: A line graph of length against time
options.rationale: Time was not measured.

explanation: Cob length shows continuous variation. The modal class (the class with the highest frequency, 15 cobs) is 16.0–18.9 cm. Cobs of 19.0 cm or longer: 10 + 4 = 14 of 40, which is 35%. Water, mineral ions, light, competition and pests all affect growth. Continuous data are drawn as a histogram.
workedSolution:
1. (a) A range of lengths with intermediates: continuous.
2. (b) The largest frequency is 15, in the 16.0–18.9 cm class.
3. (c) Cobs of 19.0 cm or more $= 10 + 4 = 14$; $\dfrac{14}{40} \times 100 = 35\%$.
4. (d) For example: water and mineral ions in the soil.
5. (e) Histogram, bars touching.
hints: The modal class has the largest number of cobs.
Add the numbers in the last two classes for (c).

stem:
A school in Bulawayo recorded the blood groups of 50 volunteers.

| Blood group | A | B | AB | O |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of people | 15 | 9 | 3 | 23 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of these volunteers who had blood group O.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which type of variation do these results show?

options.content: Continuous variation
options.rationale: There are only four categories, with nothing in between.

options.content: Environmental variation
options.rationale: Blood group is not affected by the environment.

options.content: No variation, because everyone has a blood group
options.rationale: The people differ in which group they have: that is variation.

options.content: Discontinuous variation
options.rationale: Four distinct phenotypes with no intermediates.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why there are no people with blood groups in between A and B, and why diet cannot change a person's blood group.

points.description: Blood group is controlled by one gene (with alleles $\text{I}^\text{A}$, $\text{I}^\text{B}$ and $\text{I}^\text{o}$), giving only four distinct phenotypes
It is decided by the genotype only, so environmental factors such as diet have no effect

parts.explanation: Blood group is controlled by a single gene with three alleles, so only four distinct phenotypes are possible and there are no intermediates. The phenotype is decided by the genotype alone; environmental factors such as diet cannot change it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which graph should be used to show these results?

options.content: A histogram with touching bars
options.rationale: Histograms are for continuous data.

options.content: A line graph
options.rationale: A line would suggest values between the groups.

options.content: A bar chart with separate bars
options.rationale: Each blood group is a separate category.

options.content: A scatter graph
options.rationale: There is only one variable here, measured in categories.

explanation: Group O: 23 of 50 = 46%. Blood group shows discontinuous variation, controlled by one gene and not affected by the environment, and is shown on a bar chart with separate bars.
workedSolution:
1. (a) $\dfrac{23}{50} \times 100 = 46\%$.
2. (b) Four distinct groups, no intermediates: discontinuous.
3. (c) One gene, few alleles; genotype alone sets the phenotype.
4. (d) Bar chart with gaps.
hints: Percentage = number in the group ÷ total × 100.

stem: Which feature is most likely to be affected by **both** genes and the environment?

options.content: Body mass
options.rationale: Genes set a range, and diet and exercise affect where a person falls in it.

options.content: ABO blood group
options.rationale: Blood group is set by the genotype alone.

options.content: Sex
options.rationale: Sex is decided by the X and Y chromosomes.

options.content: Round or wrinkled shape of pea seeds
options.rationale: Seed shape is controlled by one gene with two alleles.

explanation: Body mass shows continuous variation: many genes and environmental factors such as diet, exercise and illness all affect it. Blood group, sex and pea seed shape are decided by genes alone.
hints: Which feature can change if a person eats more food?

stem: True or false: the ability to roll the tongue is an example of continuous variation.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite. People either can or cannot roll their tongue: two categories with no intermediates, which is discontinuous variation.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. There are two distinct categories, so tongue rolling shows discontinuous variation.

explanation: Tongue rolling has two distinct phenotypes (can or cannot) with no intermediates, so it is an example of discontinuous variation.
hints: How many categories are there?

stem: A student measured the hand spans of 120 students and drew a histogram. It rose to a single peak in the middle and fell away evenly on both sides. What does this show?

options.content: Hand span is controlled by a single gene with two alleles.
options.rationale: A single gene usually gives a few distinct categories, not a smooth bell shape.

options.content: Hand span shows discontinuous variation.
options.rationale: A smooth range with a peak in the middle is continuous variation.

options.content: Most students have either a very small or a very large hand span.
options.rationale: The peak is in the middle, so most students are near the mean.

options.content: Hand span shows continuous variation, with most students near the middle and few at the extremes.
options.rationale: A bell-shaped (normal) distribution is typical of features controlled by many genes and the environment.

explanation: A single-peaked, bell-shaped histogram is a normal distribution, typical of continuous variation: most individuals are close to the mean and few are at either extreme. Such features are usually controlled by many genes and the environment.
hints: Where are most of the students on the histogram?

stem: Describe how you would investigate the variation in leaf length of the msasa trees in a woodland, and how you would present your results. [5]

points.description: Collect a large sample (e.g. at least 30 leaves) chosen at random, from several trees of the same species
Choose comparable leaves (e.g. fully grown leaves from similar positions) and measure the same way each time
Measure each leaf with a ruler in the same way (e.g. from the base of the leaf stalk to the tip), to the nearest mm, and record in a table
Group the lengths into equal, non-overlapping class intervals and count the frequency (tally) in each
Draw a histogram (bars touching) of frequency against leaf length; calculate the mean and range
Safety / care: do not damage the trees more than needed; collect fallen or few leaves from each tree

answerSpec.modelAnswer: I would collect a large sample of at least 30 fully grown leaves, chosen at random from several msasa trees, taking a few from each tree and from similar positions on the branches so that the leaves are comparable. I would measure each leaf with a ruler in the same way, from the base of the leaf stalk (where it joins the twig) to the tip of the leaf, to the nearest millimetre, and record the lengths in a table. I would then group the lengths into equal class intervals that do not overlap, count how many leaves fall in each class, and draw a histogram with the bars touching. I would also calculate the mean and the range of the lengths.

explanation: A good investigation uses a large random sample, measures consistently, groups the data into equal classes and presents continuous data as a histogram.
hints: How many leaves, chosen how?
Which graph suits continuous data?

stem: Compare continuous variation and discontinuous variation. Include their causes, how they are shown on a graph, and an example of each. [6]

points.description: Continuous: a range of phenotypes between two extremes, with intermediates
Discontinuous: a limited number of distinct phenotypes with no intermediates
Continuous is caused by many genes and the environment
Discontinuous is usually caused by genes only (often a single gene); little environmental effect
Continuous shown as a histogram with touching bars; discontinuous as a bar chart with separate bars
A correct example of each, e.g. height or mass (continuous) and blood group, sex or tongue rolling (discontinuous)

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Continuous variation gives a range of phenotypes between two extremes, with many intermediates, for example height or body mass. It is caused by many genes acting together with the environment, such as diet. It is shown on a histogram, whose bars touch, often forming a bell-shaped curve.

Discontinuous variation gives a limited number of distinct phenotypes with no intermediates, for example ABO blood group or tongue rolling. It is usually caused by genes alone, often a single gene, and the environment has little or no effect. It is shown on a bar chart with gaps between the bars.

explanation: The two kinds differ in the number of phenotypes, their causes and the graph used.
hints: Compare: number of phenotypes, causes, graph, examples.

stem: Which pair of features are **both** examples of discontinuous variation?

options.content: Height and body mass
options.rationale: Both vary continuously.

options.content: Leaf length and blood group
options.rationale: Leaf length varies continuously.

options.content: Tongue rolling and arm length
options.rationale: Arm length varies continuously.

options.content: Sex and ABO blood group
options.rationale: Both fall into distinct categories with no intermediates.

explanation: Sex (male or female) and ABO blood group (A, B, AB or O) both have a few distinct categories with no intermediates.
hints: Both features must fall into separate groups.

stem: The heights of ten students, in cm, were: 151, 163, 158, 170, 149, 166, 160, 155, 172 and 156. Calculate the mean height.
explanation: Total $= 1600\ \text{cm}$; mean $= 1600 \div 10 = 160\ \text{cm}$.
hints: Add the heights and divide by the number of students.
